slice: A29 parity — one handle namespace, account-scoped retroactive blocks, threaded mirror
register_row: INT-05 is NOT re-scored and NOT flipped. This slice is the owner's ruling on the two sub-clauses of INT-05's own procedure that the 2026-09-08 rehearsal left open — the handle/actor collision that made a per-remote-account block address the wrong actor, and a blocked account's already-stored content staying visible — plus the six smaller findings that rehearsal recorded without fixing. Only the third two-instance run can flip the row.
verdict: IMPLEMENTED AND UNIT/INTEGRATION-PROVEN, NOT LAB-OBSERVED. Code-only by instruction: another executor holds the machine's lab and Docker. Every claim below is a test, a migration applied to a real PostgreSQL, or an explicit statement that something was not measured. Nothing here has been seen federating between two live instances.

prs.vidra-user: https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-user/pull/202 — draft, and it STAYS draft until core merges: lib/api/generated.ts is regenerated from core's branch spec, so contract-ci cannot go green first

sc1_one_handle_namespace.rule: An account username and a channel handle reserve each other, case-insensitively under lower() — the same normalisation users_username_lower_idx and channels_handle_lower_idx have always used, so the reservation cannot disagree with the per-table uniqueness that predates it.
sc1_one_handle_namespace.enforcement: actor_handles: one row per live handle, handle_lower PRIMARY KEY, with cascading user_id/channel_id FKs (exactly one set) so a deletion releases the name with no application code. Two AFTER triggers on users(username) and channels(handle) upsert the row, arbitrating on the SUBJECT index so a rename MOVES the reservation while a cross-kind collision raises on actor_handles_pkey.
sc1_one_handle_namespace.why_after_triggers: A same-kind duplicate must keep raising on users_username_lower_idx / channels_handle_lower_idx, which are checked at INSERT time before any AFTER trigger runs. Every 409 message that shipped before 0142 is byte-identical after it; only the CROSS-kind collision is the new refusal.

surfaces.oauth_and_atproto_username_derivation: UsernameExists now probes actor_handles rather than users, so a derived username that dodged every account and landed on a CHANNEL handle is skipped by the dedupe loop instead of being refused at INSERT — a first sign-in must not become a conflict the person cannot act on
surfaces.registration_approval: 409 handle_reserved (the pending-request insert itself does not fire the trigger; a username taken by a user was ALREADY caught at approval time, and this follows that shipped behaviour)
surfaces.username_change: no endpoint exists; the trigger fires on UPDATE OF username, so the guard is in place before the endpoint that would need it
surfaces.channel_handle_change: no endpoint exists (the handle is immutable); the trigger fires on UPDATE OF handle for the same reason

conflict_code.why: Naming the holding kind would make each form an oracle for the other namespace — a registration form reporting 'that belongs to a channel' enumerates channels — and neither caller can act on the distinction: the remedy is the same word.

backfill.function: backfill_actor_handles() — a FUNCTION rather than an inline DO block so the rule can be exercised on a seeded collision by a test instead of only by the one run that ever executes it. Idempotent (every insert ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; the rename loop only sees channels that still collide); a re-run on an already-migrated database returns 0.
backfill.rule: The ACCOUNT wins every collision, because a username is a SIGN-IN identifier: renaming it locks a person out, while renaming a channel handle changes a URL this migration also keeps alive.
backfill.rename: <handle>-channel, then -channel-2, -channel-3, … until the name is free of the account namespace, the channel namespace AND the aliases already written.
backfill.audit: content.channel.handle_renamed, domain=content, actor_kind=system, resource_type=channel, resource_id=<uuid>, reason='from=<old> to=<new>', metadata {from,to,cause=handle_namespace_backfill}. audit_log carries no prose, so the names are structured on both sides.
backfill.measured: Seeded on a real PostgreSQL 16.15 at schema 141: user 'OwnerA' + channels 'ownera' and 'ownera-channel' → 'ownera' renamed to 'ownera-channel-2' (the first candidate was taken), the account kept 'ownera', the alias row carries is_actor_id=true, one audit row names both sides, and a second call renamed 0.

alias_semantics.for_humans: /channels/<old> and GET /api/v1/channels/{old} answer 301 to the new handle until expires_at — one year from the rename. After that the alias stops resolving and the name is free for a future channel; nothing else could claim it in the meantime, because the account that caused the rename holds the reservation.
alias_semantics.for_peers: is_actor_id marks the one alias the ActivityPub actor id is built from, and expires_at does NOT apply to it. The actor id, inbox, outbox, followers, following and publicKey.id all stay at the OLD handle; only preferredUsername follows the rename. An alias is a courtesy to humans and expires; a federated id is a promise to other servers and does not.
alias_semantics.why_not_a_channels_column: Adding actor_handle to `channels` turned every channel query whose SELECT lists the table's columns into a bespoke sqlc row type, rippling one federation concept through the whole channel service. Measured, then reverted.
alias_semantics.not_a_reservation: The account holds handle_lower in actor_handles; /accounts/<name> and /video-channels/<name> are different URL namespaces, so both answer at once without ambiguity.

tests: internal/store/actor_handles_integration_test.go — 6 tests: the channel direction, the account direction, both rename directions plus a legal rename that MOVES the reservation and releases the old name, same-kind duplicates still raising on their own constraint, a delete releasing the handle to the other kind, and the backfill on a seeded collision
internal/channel/service_test.go — a channel named after an account is ErrHandleReserved while a duplicate handle stays ErrConflict
internal/auth/service_test.go — a username held by a channel is ErrHandleReserved while a duplicate username stays ErrConflict
internal/httpapi/errors_test.go — 409 handle_reserved, byte-identical message in both directions
internal/pgconv/pgconv_test.go — the constraint-name classifier that keeps the two 23505s apart

sc2_webfinger_both_links.shape: acct:name@domain answers with the Person as rel=self and the Group as rel=alternate, both type application/activity+json. A name held by only one kind answers with exactly one link at rel=self, so a peer that understands only `self` is unaffected and the shipped single-link shape is unchanged.
sc2_webfinger_both_links.why_self_is_the_person: rel=self is singular by RFC 7033 and a bare acct: most often means an account. A peer picking BY TYPE gets the right actor either way, which is what the rel/type pair is for.
sc2_webfinger_both_links.aliases_resolve: A renamed channel's OLD name still resolves to its Group — through the alias, at the FROZEN actor id — because that is the address every existing follower holds.
tests: internal/federation/handle_namespace_test.go — both links for a colliding name; the single-link shape for account-only and channel-only names; a renamed channel's id/inbox/outbox/followers/publicKey.id frozen while preferredUsername follows the rename; attributedTo still naming the owning account; an unknown handle still ErrNotFound
internal/federation/actor_test.go and contract_fixture_test.go — the pre-existing WebFinger and PeerTube/Mastodon contract tests still pass unchanged

model.what_a_block_names: the ACCOUNT. A handle resolves through WebFinger and then UP through the Group's attributedTo; a supplied URL climbs the same edge through the actor CACHE.
model.reach: remote_actor_block_reach, a view that expands each block along remote_actors.attributed_to to every channel actor the account owns, and unions the admin's instance-wide per-actor blocks in as rows with a NULL blocker_id. One predicate answers both scopes: (rab.blocker_id = <viewer> OR rab.blocker_id IS NULL).
model.why_the_account: One block covers every channel the person owns INCLUDING the ones they have not created yet, which a per-channel row could never do.
model.attributed_to_is_same_host_only: attributedTo is text a remote server controls; a Group claiming an owner on another server would let a stranger redirect a block, or attach its actors to a well-behaved instance's account. Enforced at ingest and re-checked at resolution.
model.url_is_never_dereferenced: A handle has already cost a WebFinger fetch, so one actor fetch on that path changes nothing about what a caller can make this server do. A URL has cost nothing, and dereferencing it would turn 'block this actor' into 'make my server fetch this address' — so the URL path climbs only through the actor cache, which holds every actor whose content this instance actually has.
model.best_effort: An unresolvable or unowned actor keeps the URL it was given. A block must work against an actor that is offline, gone or refusing us — the actor most likely to be blocked — and the worst case is exactly the block that was already possible.

admin_surface.why_not_beside_the_instance_blocklist: An instance block is a judgement about a SERVER and takes every creator on it; this is a judgement about one PERSON. It mounts with the federation service because it resolves its identity through the same WebFinger + SSRF-guarded machinery the viewer surface does.
admin_surface.audit: moderation.remote_actor.block / .unblock, resource_type=remote_actor, resource_id=<actor url>. The moderator's note stays on the row and out of the trail — audit_log carries no prose.
admin_surface.idempotency: A re-block with an empty reason keeps the first note.

sc3_block_resolves_the_account.contract: RemoteVideo gains actor_url (the channel actor), account_actor_url (the owner — what a block should name) and channel_handle (preferredUsername@domain, the identity a viewer recognises). Before them the remote watch view carried domain, object_url and watch_url and no actor identity at all.
sc3_block_resolves_the_account.frontend: The remote watch page's control row gains 'Block account', beside Report and Mute instance. It sends account_actor_url when the origin named an owner and actor_url otherwise, unblocks with the SAME url verbatim, and is hidden for anonymous viewers and for rows that carry no actor.
tests: internal/federation/a29_parity_test.go — a channel actor resolves to its owning account; an uncached actor is neither fetched nor failed

internal/httpapi/admin_remote_blocks_test.go — 3 tests: moderator-only (401/403/200), the block→list→unblock flow with the first reason kept, and 422 for empty/plaintext/local identities and a missing actor on the DELETE

components/RemoteWatchView.test.tsx — 4 tests against the contract's own RemoteVideo type: it blocks the OWNING ACCOUNT, falls back to the channel actor when the origin named no owner, undoes with the same url, and offers nothing to an anonymous viewer or for a row with no actor

A remote actor cannot be a notification subject here: notifications key on users.id and a remote commenter has author_id NULL, so there is no remote notification row to filter. Stated rather than tested.

RECORDED, not widened into this slice. Core's own SearchPublicVideos feed query does carry the reach predicate.
tests: internal/store/remote_block_reach_integration_test.go — 2 tests on a real PostgreSQL: a viewer's block of an ACCOUNT hides its own comment, the comment from the CHANNEL it owns and the channel's video, with readback before AND after, other viewers and anonymous unaffected, and every row restored on the unblock; then the admin block doing the same for the blocker's neighbour, an anonymous reader and any signed-in viewer, with the inbound gate refusing the CHANNEL of an instance-blocked account

a_threaded_mirror.was: storeRemoteVideoNote resolved the thread with GetRemoteVideoByURL(inReplyTo), so ONLY a Note replying to the video object was mirrored. Every deeper reply was delivered successfully and dropped silently — the rehearsal watched it happen twice in one run.
a_threaded_mirror.now: remote_video_comments.parent_object_url carries the ORIGIN's object id of the parent, because replies arrive in any order and a self-referencing FK would refuse a reply whose parent has not arrived. The origin-authority check still runs against the VIDEO's origin, so a third instance cannot answer into a thread it does not host. RemoteVideoComment.parent_object_url is on the contract; a client that cannot find the parent renders the reply at the top level.

b_pending_follow_forever.was: A Reject DELETED the sender's row, making a refusal indistinguishable from a follow that was never made — and a Follow refused during an instance block gets no Reject at all, so the row sat 'pending' forever with neither side re-attempting.
b_pending_follow_forever.now: remote_channel_follows.state gains 'rejected' — terminal and creator-visible. Re-following the same actor re-arms the row to 'pending' with a NEW Follow activity id: one deliberate retry by the person whose follow it is, and the only path back for the blocked case. The shipped states are pending | accepted | rejected.

c_last_delivered_at.was: computed in cmd/api on every probe and rendered into nothing
c_last_delivered_at.now: ComponentStatus gains an optional `detail` map; the federation component sets pending, dead_lettered and — only when something has been delivered — last_delivered_at as RFC 3339. Absent rather than zero on an instance that has never delivered anything. Rendered on the AdminSystemStatusView card under the row, on healthy AND failing cards, with 'never' when absent. /admin/system's components now share ComponentStatus with /readyz; the inline copy had drifted.

d_worker_queued_request_ids.was: a worker's context is a background one and carries no request, so every federation delivery the transcode-completion hook queued recorded an empty request_id and correlation_id on BOTH the queue row and its projected run
d_worker_queued_request_ids.now: jobtrace.Recorder.RunContext reads the originating ids back off the run the worker is executing and puts them on the context, alongside the parent-job marking uploadfinalize already did. Wired into the transcode completion hook (which is what queues the deliveries) and into uploadfinalize. A live request on the context wins; an unknown run invents nothing.

e_tombstone_etag.why_it_matters_more_than_meaninglessness: An ETag invites If-None-Match, and a 304 on a 410 would tell the peer that what it already holds — the video — is current.

f_percent_encoded_domain.was: DELETE /admin/instances/blocked/127.0.0.1%3A28080 → 422 invalid domain, while the raw colon worked. Echo hands back the RAW path segment.
f_percent_encoded_domain.now: domainParam() percent-decodes the segment on the mute, unmute and unblock routes; both spellings are the same request. An undecodable segment passes through unchanged so the validator still refuses it with the message it already has.

unverified: NOTHING HERE HAS FEDERATED. No two-instance run, no browser, no Caddy: this slice is code-only by instruction because another executor holds the lab and Docker.
The 301 alias redirect is implemented in the data model and its resolution is tested, but no HTTP client has followed one.
Interoperability: no PeerTube or Mastodon has seen a two-link WebFinger answer. Both accept a single rel=self link, which is what a name held by one kind still returns.
The backfill has run only against seeded fixtures, never against beta's real data.
MIG-06's identity clause, signed fetch on the object routes and F8 authoring all stay deferred, unchanged.
what_the_third_two_instance_run_must_pro: A viewer on B blocks @name@A from the remote watch page's own control, and A's channel videos AND its already-stored comments leave that viewer's surfaces — while another viewer on B still sees both.
The same block, taken by B's admin at /admin/federation/blocked-actors, hides them for an anonymous reader too, and the unblock restores every row.
A's WebFinger answers a colliding name with both links, and B follows the GROUP from it — the request the rehearsal watched sit 'pending' forever.
A reply to a mirrored comment lands on B and renders under its parent, not at the top level.
A Reject leaves B's row 'rejected' rather than gone, and re-following sends a fresh Follow.
A private and an unlisted upload still produce ZERO activities (core #209's clause, merged and unchanged here).
/admin/system's federation card shows a real last_delivered_at, and /admin/jobs shows a request id on a delivery queued by a transcode completion.
The 410 Tombstone carries no ETag through the edge, and DELETE /admin/instances/blocked/<host%3Aport> answers 204.
unrelated_findings: SystemStatus.components described its rows inline in api/openapi.yaml rather than $ref-ing ComponentStatus, and the two had already drifted — the inline copy knew only status and error. Fixed here because the generated client could not otherwise see the new field.
UsernameExists probed only `users`, so OAuth/ATProto username derivation could land on a channel handle. It probes the shared namespace now.

A pending registration REQUEST is still only checked against the channel namespace at APPROVAL time, not at submission — the same behaviour a username already taken by a user has always had there. Left as it is, and stated.
Local blocks and mutes of remote actors: muted_accounts.muted_id is still a users FK, so there is no per-remote-account MUTE, only a block. Not in scope and not changed.

schema_compat_collision.verdict: OPEN — needs an owner ruling. This slice does not resolve it and does not weaken either rule to hide it.
schema_compat_collision.what_is_red: vidra-core's `prev-release-against-new-schema` lane (schema-compat.yml), which is part of `ci-required`. It applies HEAD's migrations to a fresh database and then runs the PREVIOUS RELEASE TAG's own integration suite against it. v0.6.2's `internal/store/search_filters_integration_test.go` seeds a channel whose handle EQUALS its owner's username — the exact collision 0142 refuses — so it fails at `actor_handles_pkey`.
schema_compat_collision.why_it_is_not_a_bug_in_this_slice: It is the policy working. The one-release schema-compat policy says release N-1's CODE must keep running against release N's SCHEMA, and `migrate-lint` spells out the additive half of it: add tables/columns/indexes, WIDEN CHECKs, RELAX NOT NULL. Unifying two namespaces is a TIGHTENING by construction — you cannot promise that the old code may keep creating collisions in a namespace whose whole point is that collisions are invalid.
schema_compat_collision.measured_consequence_of_a_rollback: Not a crash and not data loss. v0.6.2 maps 23505 through `pgconv.IsUniqueViolation` at both sites, so against the new schema it answers 409 'channel handle already taken' where it used to answer 201, and 409 'username or email already taken' on the account side. A rolled-back instance stays up and only refuses a handle that collides across the namespace — which is the thing this ruling declares invalid anyway. The failing lane is v0.6.2's own FIXTURE asserting the old permissiveness, not a broken read or write path.
the_two_options_costed: ACCEPT THE BREAK: merge as is, and record in deploy/README.md's release policy that 0142 is a deliberate one-release compat break whose only effect on N-1 is a 409 in place of a 201 for a cross-namespace handle. Cost: the executable policy has a documented exception, and the lane stays red until v0.6.3 becomes N-1.

STAGE IT OVER TWO RELEASES: release N ships actor_handles, the backfill, the aliases and the triggers that MAINTAIN the reservation, with the refusal in the APPLICATION only; release N+1 adds the unique key. Cost: for one release the database does not guarantee the namespace — which is precisely the guarantee SC1 asked for, and precisely the hole the rehearsal found (a channel taking an existing username answered 201). A reservation table that can silently under-report is the kind of safety feature this codebase rejects on principle.
schema_compat_collision.not_done_deliberately: The workflow was not touched (vidra-core AGENTS.md rule 7), the constraint was not weakened, and no session-variable trapdoor was added to let N-1 write past the trigger — a guarantee that a missing GUC silently removes reads as protection and is not.
schema_compat_collision.unrelated_flake_seen_in_the_same_lane: TestSearchSortAndFilterBehaviourAgainstPostgres/sorts_order failed on ONE of the seven runs of this lane and passed on the others, with the same tree. A relevance tie-break flake in v0.6.2's suite, not caused by this slice.
